name: Paul the Apostle
info: Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a first-century Jewish Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus to non-Jewish communities in Asia Minor and Europe and whose letters form a large part of the New Testament.

facts.born: c. 5 CE (probably between 5 BCE and 5 CE) at Tarsus in the Roman province of Cilicia; from a devout Jewish family of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, and by Acts a Roman citizen from birth
facts.died: c. 64 or 65 CE, probably at Rome, after the Great Fire of Rome in July 64 and before the last year of Nero's reign; early writers say he was martyred, and later tradition says he was beheaded
facts.role: Christian apostle and missionary to the gentiles, founder of churches in Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s CE, and author of seven undisputed letters of the New Testament; also a tent-maker by trade, according to Acts
facts.known: conversion on the road to Damascus; three missionary journeys; the Council of Jerusalem; the letters to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians and others; the argument that gentiles need not be circumcised; salvation by grace through faith; martyrdom at Rome

t: Paul was a Pharisee who persecuted the early followers of Jesus, then, after an experience on the road to Damascus, became the apostle who carried the message to non-Jewish communities around the Mediterranean.
He argued that gentile converts did not need to be circumcised or follow the Mosaic law, and his letters, seven of which scholars accept as his own, are among the earliest Christian writings.

Scholars disagree whether he was a faithful Jew, as the Paul Within Judaism approach holds, or the second founder of Christianity, and Judaism, Islam and Gnostic groups have each read him differently.
dyk: It has been estimated that Paul travelled over 12,000 kilometres by land and over 8,000 kilometres by sea on the journeys recorded in the Acts of the Apostles alone.
ev: Paul is born at Tarsus in Cilicia, probably between 5 BCE and 5 CE
After persecuting Christians he is converted on the road to Damascus, as Acts tells it
With Barnabas he makes the first missionary journey, to Cyprus and southern Asia Minor, by the traditional dating
At the Council of Jerusalem Peter, James and John accept his mission to the gentiles
He reaches Corinth, where he founds the church and stays eighteen months
In Greece he dictates the Epistle to the Romans
He goes to Jerusalem with a collection of money and is arrested in the Temple
He arrives in Rome after a shipwreck at Malta and spends two years under house arrest

sections.early:
Paul, born Saul, was probably born between 5 BCE and 5 CE at Tarsus, a trading city of the Roman province of Cilicia known for its academy. His family was devout and Jewish; he called himself of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews and a Pharisee, born of Pharisees. Acts says he was a Roman citizen by birth, and scholars largely accept this, though no source tells how his family gained it. Saul was perhaps named for the biblical King Saul, of the same tribe, while Paulus was a second name for use among Greeks and Romans, not a result of his conversion as is commonly believed.

Acts says he worked as a tent-maker or leather worker and was sent to Jerusalem to study under Gamaliel, though modern scholarship doubts he was preparing to become a scholar of the law. A sister's son is mentioned in Acts. His first language was probably Aramaic, but he wrote in Koine Greek. Before his conversion he persecuted early Christians beyond measure, by his own account, and he took part in the martyrdom of Stephen. James Dunn suggests that he targeted the Greek-speaking Hellenists in Jerusalem, because of their anti-Temple attitude.
sections.rise:
According to Acts, Saul was on his way to arrest Christians in Damascus when he saw a bright light, fell to the ground and heard a voice say, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" and "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." He was blind for three days until Ananias of Damascus laid hands on him, and he was then baptized and began at once to proclaim in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. This account occurs only in Acts, not in his letters, where he says that God was pleased to reveal his son to him. His conversion has been dated to 31 to 36 CE.

Paul says he went to Arabia, returned to Damascus and, three years after his conversion, visited Jerusalem, where he stayed with Peter for fifteen days. He claimed a gospel received by revelation, not from men. Barnabas later brought him to Antioch, where followers of Jesus were first called Christians and from which the mission to the gentiles began. Around 45 to 46 Paul and Barnabas took famine relief from Antioch to Jerusalem. Acts says the believers had been scattered after the death of Stephen, and Antioch had a large Jewish community and many gentile God-fearers.
sections.deeds:
Acts arranges his travels into three missionary journeys. The first, with Barnabas, went from Antioch to Cyprus and southern Asia Minor, and by the traditional dating took place in 46 to 49. At the Council of Jerusalem, about 49, Peter, James and John, whom Paul calls the Pillars, accepted his mission to the gentiles on the question of circumcision. On the second journey, from late 49, he parted from Barnabas, took Silas and later Timothy, preached in Philippi, Athens and before the Areopagus, and in Corinth founded a church where he stayed about eighteen months.

On the third journey he stayed almost three years at Ephesus, probably working as a tent-maker, until riots over the goddess Artemis forced him out. He then spent three months in Greece in 56 to 57, where scholars agree he dictated Romans. He also wrote to the churches of Corinth, Galatia, Philippi and Thessalonica and to Philemon. He held that Christ's death and resurrection reconciled sinners and gentiles with God, that salvation is by grace through faith, and that gentile converts need not be circumcised or follow Jewish dietary laws.
sections.opponents:
Paul met resistance from several sides. In Galatians he describes a public clash at Antioch, where he opposed Peter to his face over eating with gentile Christians, and even Barnabas sided with Peter. The Catholic Encyclopedia suggests Paul won the argument, but L. Michael White concludes that it was a failure after which Paul left Antioch for good. Paul and Barnabas later quarrelled over taking John Mark with them and separated.

Acts tells of opposition from some Jews in the cities he visited, from the silversmiths of Ephesus, and from a mob in Jerusalem in 57 who accused him of defiling the Temple by bringing gentiles into it. According to Acts a plot of 40 men against him was uncovered by his nephew. Scholars also dispute him. F. C. Baur argued that he was in violent opposition to the original twelve apostles, while Hyam Maccoby held that the Paul of Acts differs from the Paul of the letters.

Later critics charged that he corrupted or hijacked Christianity, and that he differs from Jesus in message and practice, so that he was a second founder of the faith. Early Muslim writers said he altered the teaching of Jesus. Others, among them Daniel Boyarin, read him as a Jewish thinker who lived and died convinced he was a Jew. His remarks on women and on homosexuality are still debated, and most scholars regard 1 Timothy as not his.
sections.last:
In 57 Paul arrived in Jerusalem for the fifth and last time with a collection of money for the community there. James and the elders had warned him that he was said to teach Jews to abandon Moses, and he underwent a purification ritual. Even so he was seized by a mob and placed in chains by Roman soldiers. When he asserted his Roman citizenship he escaped flogging. He was sent under escort to Caesarea, where Felix kept him for two years until Porcius Festus succeeded him, and Paul then appealed to Caesar.

Acts tells of a shipwreck at Malta, where the islanders showed him kindness, and an arrival at Rome about 60. There he spent two years under house arrest, preaching from a rented home, with which Acts ends. It does not mention his death. His death is believed to have followed the Great Fire of Rome in July 64 and to have come before 68. Clement of Rome says he bore his testimony before the rulers and Ignatius says he was martyred. Eusebius says he was killed in Nero's persecution, and Sulpicius Severus says he was beheaded. A tradition holds that he was beheaded where San Paolo alle Tre Fontane now stands. Some traditions say he went to Spain, which scholars call conjectural.
sections.legacy:
Paul's influence on Christian thinking has arguably been greater than that of any other New Testament author. 13 of its 27 books name him as author, and seven are almost universally accepted as his own; Ephesians, 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are widely regarded as written in his name, and Colossians and 2 Thessalonians are debated. His letters contain the earliest mention of the Lord's Supper and gave later thinkers their material: Augustine of Hippo drew on Romans for his work on grace, original sin and predestination, Martin Luther's reading of Romans shaped sola fide and the Reformation, and Karl Barth rewrote his commentary on Romans in 1922.

Marcion, at Rome around 144, held that Paul alone had rightly understood Christ. Gnostics prized his letters, and Valentinians claimed descent from Paul. Judaism took little interest in him until the 18th and 19th centuries, and Jewish writers such as Heinrich Graetz and Martin Buber saw him as a barrier, others such as Claude Montefiore as a bridge. Muslim writers from al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar to Ibn Taymiyya depict him as having altered the teaching of Jesus.

His tomb is held to lie under the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls; a sarcophagus inscribed PAULO APOSTOLO MART was found there in 2002. He is the patron saint of Malta, which keeps 10 February as a public holiday, and is remembered on 25 January and 29 June.

summary: Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a Pharisee who persecuted the early Christians and then became the apostle to the gentiles, founding churches around the Mediterranean and writing letters that shaped Christian theology. He is traditionally held to have been martyred at Rome under Nero.
